title: Setting Up Your MLOps Toolchain and Workflow
summary: Set up a reproducible local MLOps development environment by installing and configuring Git, Python with virtual environments, Docker, and supporting tools, then wire them together into a coherent day-to-day workflow.
objectives: Install and verify Git, Python, and Docker on a local workstation
Create isolated, reproducible Python environments using venv and pip/requirements files
Configure Git with a sensible .gitignore and commit workflow for ML projects
Build and run a minimal Docker container for an ML workload
Describe how the core tools map to stages of the MLOps lifecycle and combine into a daily workflow

quiz.q: Why should you copy requirements.txt into the Docker image before copying the rest of your code?
options: It reduces the final image size
It lets Docker cache the dependency-install layer so rebuilds are faster
It is required by the Dockerfile syntax
It prevents secrets from leaking into the image
quiz.why: Docker caches layers; copying requirements first means the expensive pip install layer is only rebuilt when dependencies change, not on every code edit.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to handle large datasets and model weights in an ML project?
options: Exclude them via .gitignore and track them with DVC or object storage
Store them inside the Docker image
quiz.why: Git is poor at large binaries. You gitignore them and use tools like DVC or object storage, tracking only lightweight pointers/metadata in Git.

quiz.q: Why create a per-project Python virtual environment instead of installing packages globally?
options: It isolates and pins dependencies for reproducibility per project
It is the only way to use pip
quiz.why: A venv isolates each project's dependencies and versions, preventing conflicts and enabling reproducible installs from a frozen requirements file.

quiz.q: Which command confirms that the Docker daemon is actually working after installation?
quiz.why: docker --version only prints the client version; docker run hello-world pulls and runs a container, proving the daemon and runtime work end to end.

quiz.q: In one short phrase, what is the central MLOps theme that connects venvs, requirements files, and Docker?
quiz.why: All three tools exist to make environments and runs reproducible across machines and team members, which is the core goal of MLOps foundations.

quiz.q: Name one tool you would use to track ML experiments (metrics, parameters, runs).
quiz.why: MLflow (or Weights & Biases) is commonly used to track experiment parameters, metrics, and artifacts across runs.

body_markdown:
## Why a Standard Toolchain Matters

MLOps lives at the intersection of data science, software engineering, and operations. Before you can train, version, deploy, or monitor models, you need a reliable, reproducible local environment. A consistent toolchain reduces the classic *"it works on my machine"* problem and gives every engineer the same baseline.

The four foundations we configure in this lesson are:

- **Git** — version control for code, configuration, and pipeline definitions.
- **Python** — the dominant language for ML, managed with isolated environments.
- **Docker** — containerization so workloads run identically anywhere.
- **Supporting CLI tools** — package managers, a code editor, and ML utilities.

## Installing and Verifying the Core Tools

Start by confirming each tool is present and on a supported version. Run these in a terminal:

```bash
git --version       # expect 2.30+
python3 --version   # expect 3.10+
docker --version    # expect 20.10+
docker run hello-world  # confirms the Docker daemon works
```

If any command fails, install via your platform: `apt`/`brew` for Git and Python, and Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) or Docker Engine (Linux). On Linux, add your user to the `docker` group so you don't need `sudo`.

## Configuring Git for ML Projects

Set your identity once, globally, then create a project-scoped `.gitignore` so you never commit large or secret artifacts:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

A good ML `.gitignore` excludes virtual environments, data, model binaries, and caches:

```gitignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
data/
models/
*.ckpt
.env
.ipynb_checkpoints/
```

Large datasets and model weights should **not** live in Git directly — use tools like DVC or object storage and track only pointers/metadata.

## Isolated Python Environments

Never install project dependencies into the system Python. Create a per-project virtual environment so dependency versions are pinned and reproducible:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install scikit-learn pandas
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Commit `requirements.txt` (or a lockfile from tools like `pip-tools`, Poetry, or `uv`) so teammates and CI install the exact same versions. Reproducibility is the central theme of MLOps.

## A Minimal Dockerized ML Workload

Docker packages your code *and* its environment into an image that runs the same on a laptop, CI runner, or cluster. A simple `Dockerfile` for a Python ML app:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "train.py"]
```

Build and run it:

```bash
docker build -t my-ml-app:dev .
docker run --rm my-ml-app:dev
```

Key practices: copy `requirements.txt` *before* the rest of the code so Docker caches the dependency layer; use slim base images; and never bake secrets into the image (pass them at runtime with `--env` or mounted files).

## How the Tools Fit the MLOps Lifecycle

| Stage | Primary tools |
|-------|---------------|
| Develop / experiment | Python, venv, Git, editor (VS Code) |
| Version data & models | DVC, object storage |
| Package & ship | Docker |
| Automate | Git + CI/CD |
| Track experiments | MLflow / Weights & Biases |

Your daily loop becomes: branch in Git → develop in an activated venv → test → build a Docker image → push and let CI validate it. Mastering this local foundation makes every later MLOps concept — pipelines, registries, deployment — far easier.

## Recap

You now have a verified, reproducible workstation: Git for versioning, a virtual environment for isolated dependencies, and Docker for portable execution. These are the non-negotiable foundations for everything that follows in the course.

slides.title: Configure Git for ML
bullets: Set name, email, and default branch globally
Add a .gitignore for envs, data, and secrets
Never commit large data or model weights
Track pointers with DVC or object storage
slides.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
slides.narration: Configure your Git identity once, globally. Then add a project gitignore that excludes virtual environments, data folders, model binaries, caches, and secret files. A core rule of MLOps: large datasets and model weights don't belong directly in Git. Instead, use tools like DVC or object storage and let Git track only the lightweight pointers and metadata.

slides.title: Isolated Python Environments
bullets: One virtual environment per project
Never install into the system Python
Pin dependencies with requirements.txt
Commit the lockfile for reproducibility
slides.code:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install scikit-learn pandas
pip freeze > requirements.txt
slides.narration: Always isolate dependencies in a per-project virtual environment, never the system Python. Create a venv, activate it, install your packages, and freeze them into requirements.txt. Commit that file — or a lockfile from pip-tools, Poetry, or uv — so teammates and CI reproduce the exact same versions. Reproducibility is the central theme here.

slides.title: A Minimal Dockerfile
bullets: Packages code AND its environment together
Copy requirements first to cache the layer
Use slim base images, keep them small
Never bake secrets into the image
slides.code:
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "train.py"]
slides.narration: Docker packages your code and its environment into an image that runs identically everywhere. Notice we copy requirements.txt before the rest of the code — this lets Docker cache the dependency layer so rebuilds are fast. Use slim base images, and pass secrets at runtime with environment variables rather than baking them into the image.

slides.title: Build and Run
bullets: Tag images clearly: name:tag
--rm cleans up the container after exit
Iterate locally before pushing to CI
Same image runs on laptop, CI, and cluster
slides.code:
docker build -t my-ml-app:dev .
docker run --rm my-ml-app:dev
slides.narration: Build the image with a clear tag, then run it. The --rm flag removes the container when it exits, keeping things tidy. The power here is portability: this exact image runs the same on your laptop, a CI runner, or a production cluster, which is why containerization is a foundation of modern MLOps.
